items.title: Komi Can't Communicate
items.description: Timid Tadano is a total wallflower, and that’s just the way he likes it. But all that changes when he finds himself alone in a classroom on the first day of high school with the legendary Komi. He quickly realizes she isn’t aloof—she’s just super awkward. Now he’s made it his mission to help her on her quest to make 100 friends! (Source: VIZ Media) Notes: - Winner of the 67th Shogakukan Manga Award in the Shounen Category in 2021. - Includes 37 extra chapters.
items.review: Komi is an absolutely charming, darling series. I’ve read about 21 volumes so far, and I love the goofy characters, the shyness, and the warm fuzzies it gives you while reading. It has a clever little art style and a cast that sticks with you, especially Najimi, whose gender seems best summed up as “Najimi,” which is wonderful. My favorite moments are when Komi gets quietly excited about seeing her friends or suddenly sprouts little cat ears. It’s a lovely high school slice of life where the power of friendship really does prevail.

items.title: The Way of the Househusband
items.description: He was the fiercest member of the yakuza, a man who left countless underworld legends in his wake. They called him “the Immortal Dragon.” But one day he walked away from it all to travel another path—the path of the househusband! The curtain rises on this cozy yakuza comedy! (Source: VIZ Media)
items.review: The Way of the Househusband is absolutely, fantastically comical. It has this rugged, ridiculous energy that I’m completely hyped about: a former yakuza legend trying to live a normal life as a househusband, while treating every grocery run, chore, and errand like it’s still some kind of mob mission. Tatsu’s tenacity to accomplish anything is genuinely admirable, and his relationship with his wife is surprisingly cute. It’s campy, pure fun, and I’m glad it became a hit because we need more of this kind of joy in life.

items.title: Mieruko-chan
items.description: One day, she could see…everything. What’s a girl to do when hideous monsters appear no matter which way she turns? And on top of that, nobody else can see them! Obviously, there’s only one thing that makes sense—ignore them. Kinda hard to put theory into practice, though, when the ghosts know she’s watching… (Source: Yen Press)
items.review: Mieruko-chan is unsettling, but I love that. Miko is the only one who can see these dark, creepy spirits, and the contrast is the whole appeal: horrifyingly ugly, disgusting ghosts crashing into the life of an absolutely adorable schoolgirl just trying to get through her day. The way she has to dissociate and keep acting normal makes you feel that same numb panic with her. If you’re up for a little fan service and some light horror-manga vibes, this is 100% your cup of tea. It hits like sweet and salty, or like grape jelly on egg toast, which maybe says something about my taste. I’ve read three or four volumes so far and watched the anime, and it’s a very nice indulgence with a great aesthetic.

items.title: Ako and Bambi
items.description: What happens when you put one down-on-his-luck amateur novelist and one amnesiac ghost girl in one bargain-priced haunted apartment? You get the punch line of Bambi’s life. The good news is, Ako is neither the ghost of the person who supposedly committed suicide in the rental nor an unfriendly poltergeist hell-bent on causing chaos. But she needs a place to hang out until she can ascend to wherever ghosts go and Bambi needs source material for his career, so maybe they can have a mutually beneficial relationship... (Source: Yen Press) Notes: -Serialization of the main storyline ended on 11 November 2021. Extra chapters are currently being selfpublished. -On 2022, the manga got licensed by the editorial Asahi Shimbun, being published under their Sonorama + Comics label.
items.review: Ako and Bambi has a very unique manga style, much less flashy than most. It’s subtle, dialogue-heavy, and the relationship building probably leans on some Japanese social idiosyncrasies that I may not totally understand. But what got me is simple: ghosts. Cute little ghost girlfriend hanging out in your room every now and then, somehow connected to another real person while neither of them really understands the other. There’s a strange little energy here. If you want to try something new, I think this is worth a go. It’s my honorable mention pick, and a reminder that there’s more to manga than the usual pattern. I’m only a couple volumes in, but I think I’m going to slow-burn this one. It has definitely opened me up to a different style. We might call you eccentric if this completely clicks for you, and honestly, that may be part of the appeal.

items.id: the girl with the sanpaku eyes
items.lookupTitle: The Girl with the Sanpaku Eyes
items.title: The Girl with the Sanpaku Eyes
items.description: Meet Amane Mizuno a girl with fierce sanpaku eyes and a pure heart! She has recently fallen for a boy named Katou, who has the exact opposite attitude! Will the tender-hearted Amane ever tell him how she feels?! (Source: Denpa) Notes: - Chapter count includes a bonus chapter. - Originally self-published on Twitter, after six chapters it was serialised by GANGANpixiv.
items.review: The Girl with the Sanpaku Eyes caught me in the store because the cover just popped. Or maybe I just love gingers. Who can say. What’s beautiful about this manga is how deliberately it uses color, with each volume leaning into a distinct palette. I’ve read three volumes so far, and while the story itself may not be the main thing I’m looking forward to, the whole book is a vibe. It feels like a piece of art more than anything: excellent coffee-table manga, and a great way to support a smaller publisher like Denpa. If you’re in it for the aesthetics, you’ve got to grab this one, because it really stands out on the shelf.

items.title: Rooster Fighter
items.description: The neighborhood cock of the walk is more than just an ordinary rooster—he’s humanity’s greatest defender! His opponents may be ten stories tall, but nothing is bigger than his stout heart and his fearsome battle cry—cock-a-doodle-doo! (Source: VIZ Media)
items.review: Rooster Fighter is so aggressive and so unbelievably ridiculous. Only Japan would give us the most badass rooster imaginable. I bought it because the gimmick was too good to ignore, and honestly, I don’t know if I’ll read past the first volume, but holy shit, what a ride. It’s striking, absurd, and weirdly brilliant as a fantasy idea. There’s so much personality baked into this rooster: his relationships with other birds, with people, with the world around him. It has a similar energy to The Way of the Househusband, with that intense, aggressive look while still knowing exactly how unserious it is. Maybe you’re like me and this kind of joke just works on you. If so, Rooster Fighter is gonna fuck you up.

items.title: Maison Ikkoku
items.description: Travel into Japan's nuttiest apartment house and meet its volatile inhabitants: Kyoko, the beautiful and mysterious new apartment manager; Yusaku, the exam-addled college student; Mrs. Ichinose, the drunken gossip; Kentaro, her bratty son; Akemi, the boozy bar hostess; and the mooching and peeping Mr. Yotsuya. Funny, touching, and a tad off-kilter, Maison Ikkoku is the great Rumiko Takahashi at her very best. (Source: VIZ Media)
items.review: Maison Ikkoku is one of the most beloved, precious stories I’ve ever gotten out of a rom-com, while still being comic genius. The whole cast is extremely well-written and constantly hilarious: embarrassing each other, spreading rumors, falling into stupid slapstick mistakes, getting drunk and screaming in the streets, classic blunders galore. Rumiko Takahashi is probably my favorite author, and this one hits so hard. It has such a period vibe that you feel like you’re living in the ’80s with them, and the apartment setting makes everyone feel oddly relatable. The characters are heightened, sure, but they still feel real enough that this could have been someone’s life. The romantic tension goes on and on for many books, and I mean that as a compliment. I’ve read the whole series, watched the whole anime, and I would do it again. It’s timeless.

items.id: shikimori s not just a cutie
items.title: Shikimori's Not Just a Cutie
items.description: Shikimori seems like the perfect girlfriend: cute, fun to be around, sweet when she wants to be… but she has a cool dark side that comes out under the right circumstances. And her boyfriend Izumi loves to be around when that happens! (Source: Kodansha USA) Notes: - Originally self-published on Twitter, was then licensed by Kodansha for serialization. - Won 5th place in Tsugimanga 2020 Award in the Web Manga Category. - Includes 25 extra chapters.
items.review: Shikimori’s Not Just a Cutie has this sweet little “small moments of endearment” thing going for it. It’s full of those relatable, cute ways you might describe your significant other when you’re seeing them in their best light. It’s basically the opposite of getting the ick, and for that, I praise it. We need more stories that look for the best in each other rather than the worst, and that appreciate those little traits enough to cherish them. It may not be the most fantastic story, but it gives you clever, affectionate moments to hang on to. I’m just getting into it, and that gentle charm is the appeal so far.

items.title: My Deer Friend Nokotan
items.description: Girl meets elk-girl—and chaos ensues! No one knows Torako used to be a delinquent. All of her classmates only know her as the perfect student. But everything changes when Nokotan, a transfer student with antlers, enters her life. Antlers aren’t the only thing strange about Nokotan. Her deer nose can sniff out Torako’s secret past! Whether it’s at school or the zoo, chaos follows this doe-eyed girl’s every step. Torako has so many questions! Is Nokotan a deer, a girl, or something in-between? (Source: Seven Seas Entertainment)
items.review: My Deer Friend Nokotan might take the cake for absurdity, and I love its cantankerous prankster energy. It gets almost upsetting to watch in the best way, because the characters are so cringe, constantly pissing each other off and getting under each other’s skin. Nokotan is a menace beyond belief. It’s a little bit much, honestly, and I haven’t gotten super deep into the series yet, but there’s already so much to appreciate about what it brings to the table. The vibes are beyond ten; they go to eleven. There’s also so much happening as an in-joke that I’m still learning how to read, and it makes me more passionate about understanding Japanese culture and language.

items.title: Goodnight Punpun
items.description: Meet Punpun Punyama. He’s an average kid in an average town. He wants to win a Nobel Prize and save the world. He wants the girl he has a crush on to like him back. He wants to find some porn. That’s what he wants, but what does he get…? (Source: VIZ Media)
items.review: Goodnight Punpun is Inio Asano being way, way out there. This is dark in a “I don’t want to think about my weird past right now” kind of way; dark in a “this is bringing up shameful memories I may not be ready to handle” kind of way. Following Punpun through life is secondhand embarrassment, childhood trauma, pain, and emotional rot, all wrapped up in this strange little bird-like figure. It’s notorious for a reason, and it feels like a love-it-or-hate-it kind of journey. If you want to open that can of worms with Oyasumi Punpun, I’m just going to warn you: it is very much its own thing.

items.title: Ran and the Gray World
items.description: Ran Uruma can't wait to grow up and become a sorceress like her mother, so with the help of a magical pair of sneakers, she transforms into an adult and sets off! Her father and older brother Jin try to keep her home safe, but Ran is determined to advance her powers and have adventures of her own! (Source: VIZ Media) Note: Includes six extra chapters.
items.review: Ran and the Gray World is a dazzling little adventure about a girl who finds magical sneakers. What more could you want? Ran is gorgeous, chaotic, and has no idea what she’s doing as she gets pulled into the adult world, seeing through adult eyes while still very much being a kid. She probably should not be talking to boys and being flirty, but, well, we’re here for the art. And the art absolutely stands out: clean, colorful, with a certain zen to it. I wouldn’t pass this one up, at least for the first volume. It’s charming, sweet, bubbly, fun, and full of magical-girl energy without going completely overboard. It has stuck with me through the years, and when I see it on someone else’s shelf, I’m impressed they picked up Aki Irie. It may not be the most compelling story, but I think it can capture your attention wholeheartedly.

items.title: Kamisama Kiss
items.description: After her father leaves her homeless Nanami ends up at a rundown shrine and is mistaken for its new local deity. Between divine duties and a sharp-tongued fox familiar her ordinary life turns into a supernatural romance.
items.review: Kamisama Kiss always feels somehow indulgent to me, like I’m reading something I’m not supposed to be reading, but I love it. The Japanese folklore flavor is a huge part of the appeal: Shinto traditions, spirits, shrines, gods, all that good stuff. It gives you that kooky supernatural energy mixed with classic shoujo emotional tension and dashingly beautiful characters. I’m not too deep into it yet, but it hits the spot every now and again, and I have a real soft spot for it. The anime also has some genuinely cute songs. If anything, the whole series feels like a little fever dream, and it’s funny how much it reminds me of Fruits Basket too: girl suddenly without a stable home, pulled into a strange household full of beautiful supernatural trouble.

items.title: Dissolving Classroom
items.description: Yuma and Chizumi drift from place to place leaving curses obsession and body horror behind them. This Junji Ito collection turns rumor and cruelty into grotesque supernatural disasters.
items.review: Dissolving Classroom just feels classic for some reason. I’ve bought at least two extra copies to give to friends, and whether they read it or not, there’s something about it that feels like the perfect little horror manga. It’s weird to call something a classic when the details get a little lost, but it has that Huckleberry Finn or Tom Sawyer quality where the exact plot beats almost matter less than the strange, lasting sense of it. This one hits that “yeah, okay, people are dissolving now, full send” spot. It doesn’t have to be overly complicated; the horror just grows stranger and nastier as it goes. For a compact Junji Ito recommendation, this one absolutely does the job.

items.title: Gyo
items.description: A nightmare plague begins with foul-smelling fish crawling onto land on mechanical legs. Junji Ito turns seaside panic into a relentless horror spiral full of rot obsession and apocalyptic dread.
items.review: What’s phenomenal about Gyo is just how visually upsetting the whole thing is, and how it keeps getting worse. A lot of horror does you the injustice of serving up something that feels stereotypically horrifying, but Junji Ito’s work here does not feel stereotypical in the least. There are sharks on insane mechanical contraptions, gas and rot and bodies, people being massacred while half the population seems to be mutating or bloating in grotesque ways. It’s indescribably unsettling. I almost put it down at one point because I usually prefer something a little more beautifully creepy, but it’s too intriguing to stop reading, no matter how disgusting it gets. If you can stomach it, Gyo is unforgettable.

items.title: Kaguya-sama: Love is War
items.description: As leaders of their prestigious academy’s student council, Kaguya and Miyuki are the elite of the elite! But it’s lonely at the top… Luckily for them, they’ve fallen in love! There’s just one problem—they both have too much pride to admit it. And so begins the daily scheming to get the object of their affection to confess their romantic feelings first… Love is a war you win by losing. (Source: VIZ Media) Notes: - The first 10 chapters were published in Monthly Miracle Jump. It switched to Weekly Young Jump starting with Ch. 11, with the chapter count being reset. This entry still includes the first 10 chapters from Miracle Jump. - Winner of the 65th Shogakukan Manga Award for "Best General Manga" category in 2019.
items.review: Kaguya-sama: Love Is War is all about clever battles. The tension comes from characters overthinking every tiny social move, and then the sudden lighthearted release when someone who has no idea what’s happening in the subtext just blurts out the obvious or ruins the whole plan. That juxtaposition is fantastic. The series pulls you in with the intrigue of each little wrapped-up moment of progression as the characters duke it out over social problems that feel extremely meaningful when you’re in high school. It also has that group-dynamics appeal you get from something like Persona, with the student council becoming its own little world of rivalries, crushes, schemes, and friendship. But if you’re just here for Chika because of her amazing dance, that’s totally fair too.

items.title: Chobits
items.description: After moving from the countryside into the big city, poor college student Hideki Motosuwa finds himself down on his luck. All he wants is a good job, a girlfriend, and his very own “persocom” - the latest and greatest in humanoid computer technology. Hideki’s luck changes one night when he finds Chi - an adorable, but seemingly broken, persocom thrown out in a pile of trash. After taking her home, Hideki discovers that Chi is more responsibility than he expected - and that there’s much more to his cute new persocom than meets the eye. (Source: Kodansha USA)
items.review: This one is for all you Clanker lovers out there. May you too find your Persocom in the trash, rescue her, and discover that she is somehow both a total blank slate and possibly the most powerful android anyone has ever seen. Chobits has that wonderfully strange setup where everyone is looking at you sideways because you’re walking around with the most gorgeous Persocom imaginable, and what you’ve got at home might secretly be some brilliant piece of advanced technology from a mysterious lab. I’m still easing my way into it, biting off and chewing a little bit at a time, but it’s a classic for a reason. The artwork is tremendous, the anime is endearing, and yes, you get to see the cute Persocom wearing many outfits.

items.title: Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End
items.description: The adventure is over but life goes on for an elf mage just beginning to learn what living is all about. Elf mage Frieren and her courageous fellow adventurers have defeated the Demon King and brought peace to the land. With the great struggle over, they all go their separate ways to live a quiet life. But as an elf, Frieren, nearly immortal, will long outlive the rest of her former party. How will she come to terms with the mortality of her friends? How can she find fulfillment in her own life, and can she learn to understand what life means to the humans around her? Frieren begins a new journey to find the answer. (Source: VIZ Media) Notes: - Winner of the Grand Prize at the 14th Manga Taisho Awards. - Nominated for the 25th Annual Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize. - Placed 3rd at the 7th Annual Next Manga Award.
items.review: Frieren is one of those series that makes quietness feel like the whole point. It has this strange pacing where you’re frolicking through the woods in a magical medieval fantasy world, solving little problems here and there, almost with Mushishi vibes, and then suddenly the whole thing shifts into a massive demon battle where heads are flying, Frieren is a total badass, and everyone is rooting for Fern. I understand why some people bounce off it as slow, but the people who love it are absolutely obsessed. What captured everyone’s heart, I think, is this endearing, beautiful grandma elf lady at the center of it all. It feels stereotypical and completely new at the same time, hiding in plain sight. Frieren made a huge dent in the current anime moment by creating a new kind of staple. It almost feels like reinventing bread.

items.title: Noragami: Stray God
items.description: Yato is a homeless god. He doesn’t even have a shrine, not to mention worshippers! So to achieve his ambitious goals, he’s set up a service to help those in need (for a small fee), hoping he’ll eventually raise enough money to build himself the lavish temple of his dreams. Of course, he can’t afford to be picky, so Yato accepts all kinds of jobs, from finding lost kittens to helping a student overcome bullies at school. (Source: Kodansha USA)
items.review: Noragami has that swashbuckler energy and shounen attitude, but it feels sleeker and more self-aware than a lot of other battle manga. It has the familiar demon-fighting setup, with a broke demigod anti-hero protagonist carrying that edgelord “I can do anything” attitude, but we love Yato anyway, warts and all. I think Noragami hits a lot of people as the shounen-adjacent series they can really stand behind: not overbearing, not too loud, and still redeemable in its whole aesthetic. It has this dark blue, sharp elegance to its design, and the humor is more understated and subtle than you might expect.

items.title: OMORI
items.description: After—something—changed his life four years ago, Sunny has not left his house once, living in his own reclusive bubble. Hoping for a fresh start for her son, his mother decides to move their family out of town. However, when his childhood friend Kel re-enters his life, Sunny finds himself thrust back into a world he once knew. With only three days before the move, the duo come across familiar faces as they go through town—reawakening a dark past that Sunny has tried so hard to forget. (Source: K Manga)
items.review: I’m still getting into OMORI, and a friend told me it comes from a game, so now I’m checking that out too. It’s super eccentric, with a definite psychological twist running underneath everything. I like that there’s already a strong cast of characters, but I’m not ready to give it a full review yet because my interest in the series is still developing. For now, it gets an honorable mention for coming from an indie game, looking so striking on the shelf, and immediately making me want to know more. The first few pages set up such a visual mystery, and the protagonist’s dark, fractured inner world is intriguing. I’m looking forward to seeing where this one goes.

items.title: Persona 5
items.description: After being arrested and sent to a new high school in Tokyo, Akira Kurusu awakens to the power of Persona and joins the Phantom Thieves to confront the twisted desires around them.
items.review: I love Persona 5 so much. I’m super obsessed with the game, and it’s basically all I’ve been playing lately, so of course I had to run out and find the manga. The cast is unbelievably well written, the aesthetic is brilliant, and the whole world feels so detailed and thought out that you could write an hour-long essay before even scratching the surface. I love how it folds in super-spy style, gentleman-thief energy, and historical fiction influences while still feeling completely modern. What strikes me most is the depth of the philosophical content and moral dilemmas. The story keeps you on edge while surrounding everything with occult and mythological imagery drawn from cultures all over the world. At the same time, the problems the characters face are relatable to the umpteenth degree: painful, emotional, and very real. The whole Persona 5 universe has me hooked.

items.id: yorha pearl harbor descent record a nier automata story
items.lookupTitle: YoRHa - Pearl Harbor Descent Record - A NieR:Automata Story
items.title: YoRHa: Pearl Harbor Descent Record – A NieR:Automata Story
items.description: In the distant future, machine lifeforms have driven humanity to the Moon. The Council of Humanity deploys the female android unit YoRHa to Earth, where they fight to recapture the planet in a story set in the world of NieR:Automata.
items.review: I’ll be honest: NieR:Automata is pure indulgence for me. I just like getting lost in this universe. It’s surreal, cerebral, and yes, we all know we’re here for 2B and her beautiful sword. YoRHa: Pearl Harbor Descent Record feels like more excellent content to scratch that itch the game leaves behind. For some reason, I can’t quite make myself completely finish the game, the anime, or even chase down more of the manga, and I think it’s because part of me doesn’t want it to end. I’m intentionally leaving blank lines to be filled in later. It’s not that I don’t love it; it’s that I’m not racing to the end on this one, and I’ve never really experienced that before. Something about the whole series has this timeless, futurist, alive energy that is worth exploring slowly, one strange little moment at a time.

items.title: Rurouni Kenshin
items.description: Himura Kenshin was once a feared assassin in the final years of the Bakumatsu. Now he wanders Meiji-era Japan with a reversed-edge sword, trying to protect people without returning to the violence that made him famous.
items.review: It almost kills me to even try to say anything about Rurouni Kenshin. It’s that remarkable to me. I have a tattoo of Himura Kenshin on my shoulder blade because he is genuinely one of my role models: the most elegant, refined, aloof, morally driven swordsman fantasy character I could ever ask for. The series is beautifully written, with a historical texture that helps you feel the transition from the Bakumatsu into the Meiji era. I’ve seen all the live-action films, watched the original anime, started the remake, and read the entire manga. It’s beautiful, bloody, challenging, and unforgettable. Kenshin lives in my heart daily as a reminder of what true heroes stand for, and how they face the darkness in the world around them and in their own minds.

items.title: Ranma ½
items.description: Ranma Saotome is a martial artist with a curse: cold water turns him into a girl, hot water turns him back, and an arranged engagement pulls him into nonstop fights, crushes, and slapstick chaos.
items.review: Ranma 1/2 is stupidly lovable and totally unexpected in every way. I first fell in love with it when I was 15 and learning kung fu, after one of my martial arts teachers told me, “You should watch Ranma 1/2. It’s a classic.” He was right. I was hooked. The martial arts are exquisitely ridiculous, the romance never quite resolves because Takahashi loves keeping people emotionally tangled forever, and every character seems built around some identity-based comic bit. Ranma switching between male and female, his father switching between man and panda, Shampoo and Mousse running around with their own absurd naming jokes: it all becomes this huge, chaotic rom-com machine. What I love is that the gender-swapping is silly, but it still brushes up against a real emotional question: what if I were the other gender, even just sometimes? It has this innocent curiosity about identity, frustration, safety, embarrassment, and performance, all wrapped in slapstick kung fu nonsense. Akane’s tomboyish energy makes the contrast even better, especially with Ranma constantly insisting she’s “not cute” while obviously being tangled up in her anyway. I love this series so much. It’s fun, uncanny, ridiculous, and completely alive.

items.title: Fullmetal Alchemist
items.description: After a forbidden alchemical ritual destroys their bodies, Edward and Alphonse Elric search for the Philosopher's Stone in a story about sacrifice, war, science, and the cost of trying to bring back what was lost.
items.review: What’s brilliant about Fullmetal Alchemist, especially as it ages into a modern classic, is how perfectly it captures something about European antiquity and Western hermetic occult tradition. That whole alchemical foundation is displayed through a remarkable cast, a deeply thoughtful philosophical plot, and two incredibly lovable leads. I don’t know anyone who has experienced this series and not fallen in love with some version of it. I’ve read through the whole manga, and I think that’s the cleanest way to experience the story, even though the anime adaptations are fantastic too. The manga lets you sink into the world, sit with it, and absorb everything it has to offer.

items.title: Death Note
items.description: Light Yagami finds a notebook that can kill anyone whose name is written inside. What starts as a private judgment fantasy turns into a tense battle of strategy between Light and the detective trying to stop him.
items.review: Here’s the thing: I have to give Death Note an honorable mention for the manga in particular. Don’t get me wrong, I love the anime as much as the next person, and yes, this is probably one of the most overcooked series I could be talking about. But collecting the manga reminded me why Death Note matters. Every volume feels like a little treasure, like a gemstone. The series had faded into the background of my memory as “yeah, that was a great one,” and pop culture had maybe tarnished its reputation a little over time. Then I picked up the first book, looked at the cover, and felt that inspiration all over again, like it was brand new. Every panel feels loaded with personality and intention. The characters are beautifully thought out, and once Misa shows up, the whole dynamic gets even more intense and visually striking. There’s something majestic about how much religious and Catholic iconography gets folded into the aesthetic: dark, dramatic, and somehow still popping off the page. Death Note stands as pure classic gold-standard anime and manga across the board.
